Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished members of the Board, Mr. Administrator, Lebanon associates itself with the statement delivered by Iraq on behalf of the G77 and China, and by Morocco on behalf of the Like-Minded Group of Middle-Income Countries. Let me start by highlighting the opportunity and the value of interacting today with the Administrator. As well, we thank him for this comprehensive overview of the UNDP ongoing efforts to deliver responsive solutions in a vulnerable world still dealing unfortunately with rising inequalities and several global challenges. We commend and value the work of the UNDP implementing a range of programs and innovative partnerships, including in crisis-affected countries and middle-income countries like Lebanon. UNDP has consistently been a strong partner for Lebanon, supporting reform and restructuring of the public sector through capacity-building programs and technical support in areas such as poverty eradication, renewable energy taxation, and digital transformation. It has also played a key role in fostering institutional capacities to support gender-responsive interventions while actively engaging civil society, women, and youth to work towards a sustainable future for a more powerful, by clean energy. Moreover, since October 2023, the Israeli aggressions and the latest war on Lebanon have generated an additional layer of complexity impacting key economic sectors with significant losses in GDP and the agricultural sector, which has reversed sustainable development acceleration with alarming consequences on the Lebanese economy, infrastructure, and the environment, as reflected in several reports by UNDP. Among the weapons, weapons used in Lebanon, white phosphorus ammunition causing significant environmental damage and harm to the ecosystem and threats to public health resulting in agricultural disasters, long-lasting consequences and economic losses, and contaminated water sources and soil. In the beginning of October 2024, the Resident Coordinator and the Lebanese government launched a flash appeal to mobilize urgent resources for civilians affected by the escalating conflict and resulting humanitarian crisis. We seize this opportunity to express our appreciation to the United Nations agencies and particularly to UNDP and the Friends of Lebanon for their support to the Lebanese government and the local authorities on service delivery. We welcome the report launched last week by UNDP Lebanon entitled From Crisis to Recovery: Local Authorities Confronting Post-War Realities in Lebanon, Rapid Impact Assessment. The report relies on data collected from municipalities and their unions, with support from disaster risk management units at the government level. It explores the impact of the Israeli aggressions and the latest war in Lebanon and the damages for a variety of assets, as 90,076 total assets were damaged in 135 surveyed areas. It focuses on displacement and many other topics also, like infrastructure damage, socioeconomic challenges. And I would like just to reflect on something, that more than 1.2 million civilians were displaced, and until now, after the cessation of hostilities agreement, some Lebanese civilians are returning to their homes, However, some damages and destruction are being reflected by many other studies done by the Lebanese government. Today, the keywords are immediate needs and reconstruction. With the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement in place since November 2024, and the election of a new president and the designation of a new prime minister to form a new government, we would like to call on UN agencies and the international community to support Lebanon and to help facilitate reconstruction.

Thank you, Mr. President, Mr. Administrator, and the distinguished board members. Allow us to also congratulate the UNDP team and the Secretariat of the Board for their tremendous and tireless efforts in conducting the session during the difficult times. We have no doubts that this session will contribute in improving the efficiency and effectiveness of the organization and to streamline better delivery of its mandate. We thank the Administrator Achim Steiner for his comprehensive statement and most importantly for his remarkable contribution to the management of this critical and complex organization and wish him continued success in his endeavors in addressing the future challenges. Mr. President, the statement highlights the challenges developing countries face, including conflicts, economic and environmental issues, and the digital divide, which hinder their recovery and progress. We emphasize the importance of multilateral efforts to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals while stressing the responsibility to foster hope in 2024. We call global collaboration to achieve the SDGs, particularly in the remaining 5 years. With a crucial responsibility ahead, alongside the recent adoption of the Q CPR, the Global Digital Compact, the upcoming Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, and the Social Summit, we are committed to making every effort over the next 5 years to fulfill the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. We urge our partners to join us in this endeavor and work towards achieving. the goals set in 2015 for the betterment of everyone. Mr. President, in India, we have demonstrated the transformation potential of digital technologies. The Digital India initiative demonstrates how digital public infrastructure can drive sustainable development and is today an example of what India can readily offer to the world. With over 1.3 billion digital identities and a globally recognized digital payments ecosystem, system driven by the Unified Payment Interface, India has made financial services accessible to millions, particularly in rural areas, fostering inclusion and reducing inequality. Mr. President, we reaffirm our continued support in the UNDP's role in global sustainable development by addressing key challenges. Thank you, Mr. President.
Thank you for your statement. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the European Union.

Thank you very much. Dear Administrator, Excellencies, and members of the Executive Board, I am delivering this statement on behalf of the European Union as a donor and would like to start by expressing our sincere condolences to the U.S. delegation following yesterday's accident. To begin, we would like to thank the Administrator for his informative update and his insightful observations. We have 3 points to make and 1 question for the Administrator. First, the EU wishes to congratulate UNDP for reaching the milestone of 60 years of operation. The EU is dedicated to continuing its longstanding collaboration with UNDP to promote sustainable, inclusive, and equitable development worldwide in an ever-changing political landscape. We have a solid partnership with UNDP at country level as well as between headquarters. The EU and EU member states are the largest contributor of funds to UNDP, which emphasizes just how vital our partnership is. Last year, we marked 20 years since the signature of the Strategic Partnership Agreement with UNDP. To mark this period of cooperation, we convened for a high-level strategic dialogue to exchange views on the global development challenges and identify ways to expand the partnership. This brings me to my second point. Putting the SDGs back on track requires unprecedented mobilization and funding from both public and private sectors. We must shift from the traditional donor-recipient paradigm to instead cultivate partnerships of equals. UNDP and the EU need to be bold as development actors exploring new opportunities for cooperation and innovative ways to address international challenges. This is why the EU launched Global Gateway, to boost smart, clean, and secure links in digital, energy, and transport, and strengthen health, education, and research systems across the world. UNDP and the EU have aligned priorities in this regard, such as promoting digital connectivity and green solutions globally. My question to the Administrator would therefore be, what innovative financing models could be integrated in the next strategic plan, taking this into consideration. Finally, as highlighted in a joint statement delivered by Belgium, we stress the importance of an effective and efficient UN system, including at country level. In this regard, we support increased alignment, integration, and collaboration among UN entities in line with the One UN approach and under the leadership of the UN Resident Coordinator. As part of this, UNDP has been and remains indispensable in advancing sustainable development on the ground in developing countries. UNDP's country presence in 170 countries and territories is a unique strength which allows access to valuable entry points with national and local authorities. This presence is proven to deliver integrated development solutions tailored to specific country priorities. In conclusion, we look forward to strengthening our relations with UNDP for the people and the planet.

Thank you. Thank you for your statement. Administrator Steiner, I'd like to offer you the floor to allow you to respond to the comments and questions you received which we heard following this morning and just now. Could you also kindly give us a general conclusion? That would be very useful I think for all of us here.

Thank you, Mr. President. I just want to make up for something I forgot this morning. To our dear colleagues from China, a happy Lunar New Year. I meant to say this this morning. And I appreciate very much that we are able to organize our board meeting even though a lot of people have actually gone into New Year's celebrations around the world. Let me again briefly pick up on a number of questions. First of all, on the strategic plan, We welcome and have noted your directions. Also this morning I did not have a chance to respond to Belgium and to others. New Zealand just provided us also with a number of inputs. This is exactly what we are looking for from you and over the next few months to be able to engage with you. And our next briefing on the strategic plan will be towards the end of February. In the meantime, to those of you who wish to consult consult or read an attempt to describe, let's say, the context out of what we have seen from Futures and Strategies work, from our surveys, the many consultations, the so-called landscape paper is now on the UNDP website. It's written in a very concise way, so I think even if you're not interested in the strategic plan, you will find it, I think, of interest in interpreting what is happening around us. Now, there was an interesting point about the right to development. We have a so-called UN Declaration on the Right to Development. It was, as those of you who have studied a little bit of history, not an easy process of negotiating it, many compromises made, but nevertheless it forms part of the fundamental discourse around rights. And I think whether a Whether a new legal instrument to be negotiated is necessarily the way forward, I think this is something that I would not want to comment on from a UNDP perspective right now because it involves many different considerations. However, what I want to be very clear about, and we always have been, we view the Declaration on the Right to Development as integral to the way we interpret the mandate of a UN organization, working on development today. And whether you individualize those rights or whether you view them also as in the context of a nation-state and a society, to have a discourse in a world where inequality also defines the ability to fulfill that right or not, where the decisions of one country on mitigating and reducing its carbon footprint will compromise or protect the rights of another nation's right to development. You know, this is some of the most fundamental thinking in jurisprudence terms that I think jurists will do for us, but in the meantime we are in a race against time and I want to emphasize again that in the way we look, for example, on actions on climate change, they are not constraining development, they must enable development, and I think UNDP, with a community of practitioners around the world, is today an organization that is deeply committed to understanding not only the threat and the imperative to mitigate or indeed to adapt, but rather how to envisage a development pathway where climate becomes a driver for innovation, for energy security, for job creation, for— in the context of particularly many African economies, the foundation for industrialization, and again to the comments of Nigeria also, we can transact this discussion through a 2030 Agenda SDG lens, as you have also done. We can do it through a right to development discourse. We can do it through the Paris Agreement lens. I think again what UNDP represents to you, and here I want to go back to something that was said this morning, UNDP cannot be everything to everyone everywhere. But UNDP is the platform on which anyone, anywhere, can engage with where development decisions will actually determine the course of a nation, a community, or indeed of the family of nations. And I think this time and again takes me to what many of you have acknowledged this morning also and again in some of the comments this afternoon, and I thank also our distinguished delegate from Bulgaria, for reminding us the ability of UNDP to respond to contemporary challenges, to be part of an innovation-driven organization, but also to be able to pivot, as we heard from Bangladesh, from one day to the other, and to have— and this is sometimes what strikes me as so remarkable— we are an institution that is working for a country and its people, and even though there was literally an ousting of one leader and the next day another leader was leading the country, UNDP was never in question as being a trusted partner. There are not many organisations in our world that literally are able to be seen as credible partners even when there is an unconstitutional or otherwise change of government, from one elected government to another. And in that sense, I again, for this discussion about UNDP's role and the strategic plan, I hope that in the next few weeks and months we can interrogate some of these assets. They are the intangibles that define why even a Board of Auditors— and I thank France for raising this earlier today— in its remarks. When the Board of Auditors examined the presence model, as we call it, the presence of UNDP across the world in terms of its project and physical team's presence, but also its platform function for the UN as a whole, a group of auditors was surprised at how underrated the value of this infrastructure is, not only to UNDP's ability to you have a unique value proposition, but actually to the UN system and, by extension, to the international community. And I say this to you because, again, in some of the comments that have now been made, you quite rightly also pointed to the fact that how do we articulate this in a strategic plan so that there is some sense of where the institution is at the forefront, maybe where the institution is more a kind of last resort, but it is not its core business. If you go back to the situation in the Red Sea and off the coast of Yemen when an oil tanker was about to sink and cause a disastrous environmental impact, this was never written into a strategic plan of UNDP and frankly I hope we do not get into the business of dealing with stranded oil tankers, but the fact that UNDP in the end was an institution that could bring all of the different actors together and essentially de-risk this time bomb that we had there is illustrative, I think, of something that we need to get a clearer understanding. I want to mention another example that has been striking. Ambassador, you are sitting here and you know this better than I do. In Ethiopia right now, there is a major demobilization and reintegration and disarmament, or rather demobilization, disarmament, and reintegration process underway. And we have been proud partners to Colombia as part of the peace process there to be integral to the DDR process, not only by collecting weapons, etc., but in fact by beginning to invest in the ability to reintegrate excombatants. Ethiopia is planning to demobilize around 370,000 combatants. It has invited UNDP to be a key partner in this exercise to now begin the demobilization and reintegration of these ex-combatants. This is an extraordinary undertaking, vital to the foundations of peace ultimately returning And therefore, I again want to illustrate to you that what is UNDP's core competence in dealing with soldiers? Well, it's not the issue that they are soldiers; it is how do we make them from combatants or soldiers, enable them to become citizens again and people who are able to earn a livelihood and be peacebuilders in their own communities. So, Mr. President, I I wanted to touch on a few of these comments and remarks that were raised just now. I cannot, again, do justice to them, but I think particularly on the strategic plan, also our commitment around the whole— and you've heard it from virtually every country this morning— the technology development interface, we are very clearly listening to what you are saying and are factoring this into, let's say, the first draft of a strategic plan that will allow you, first of all, to calibrate how UNDP is focused on the demand that is out there, how this relates to the resources that may be available to it, and how it also leverages the fact that it is an integral part of the UN development system, and I would go beyond that, the UN family. With Tom Fletcher, the Emergency Relief Coordinator, and I as head of UNDP, and us together with Rosemary DiCarlo and others, We are continuously coordinating our response. When you look at a situation like Syria now, UNDP is one of the most present organizations on the ground. We are actively working, before what happened in the last few weeks, in 14 governorates. Our ability to be a stabilizing factor, but also together with UNHCR to look at the return of refugees, to quickly look at stabilizing a, let's say, government in turmoil and the ability to stabilize, the ability to function as a government are again integral elements of UNDP's ability to complement a political engagement on the part of the UN, a humanitarian engagement on the part of the UN, but ultimately, as we have put on the front doors of our building, there is no peace without development and there will be no development without peace. And that is where I close the circle, as you have asked me to, with human development and what it is that we represent within the United Nations family, first of all, but also in our presence in so many of your countries as more than just an aspiration, more than just a declaration, more than just a commitment to each other. We are a real-life expression of working together with one another on the development of each individual country and by that being able to achieve perhaps that aspirational right to development, the Paris Agreement and so many other milestones along the way. And I want to remember, in Brazil we began a journey on sustainable development in 1992. That journey continues to this day. And I think UNDP, as part of the UN development system, will be at the heart of that capacity of the UN to be relevant to where the world wants to work together, while holding up sometimes the principles of what the world should be doing but is not yet ready to do, and recognize why it matters. With that, I hope I have responded adequately to some of the overarching themes, and again, in my written responses to you, we will also speak more to the financing issue, to the questions of the relationship between the Resident Coordinator, the UN Country Team, and UNDP. But please take with you the very clear commitment from us. We are not some franchise operation. We are an integral part of the United Nations. We see ourselves as integral to the UN system, but we are also very conscious of the unique value and role that this institution represents to the international community, and being able to live up to that every day in what we do has to be our guiding yardstick.

Thank you.

And I think the applause says everything, Administrator Steiner. Mr. President, distinguished members of the Executive Board, Good afternoon. It is my pleasure to present the main results of the independent evaluation of the UNFPA Strategic Plan, which incorporated innovative elements including coordinating with 6 concurrent regional program evaluations to avoid duplication, create synergies, and increase efficiency, and leveraging ethical and responsible artificial intelligence in the data collection, in addition to be very timely to inform the design of the next Strategic Plan. Mr. President, distinguished delegates, please allow me to present the 5 conclusions and recommendations from the evaluation. First, successive Strategic Plans aiming for the 3 transformative results provided continuity and focus but require adaptability, with acceleration remaining relevant yet potentially insufficient for countries facing setbacks. Despite some long-term improvements, recent data reveals uneven progress. Many countries require significant acceleration, while others need to prevent backsliding. The evaluation recommends, within the overarching framework of the 3 transformative results, ICPD Programme of Action and the SDGs; to focus the next Strategic Plan on further acceleration, rather than unfinished business; and ensure that efforts to protect the ICPD agenda are fully integrated into the approach. Second, the 3 transformative results effectively focus UNFPA resources on key priorities, but they do not fully encompass stakeholders' needs or the Organization's broader contribution to the SDGs and to the ICPD Programme of Action, particularly in areas such as population dynamics, gender equality, HIV, and youth. The Strategic Plan's theory of change doesn't capture these direct contributions. Instead, it shows them flowing solely through the Trilateral transformative results without recognizing the diverse pathways UNFPA utilized to achieve these results. The evaluation recommends the next Strategic Plan to clarify UNFPA's strategic positioning in population dynamics and other key areas, and their direct contribution to the ACPD and SDGs. Third, the Strategic Plan shifts demanded substantial organizational efforts. requiring clear guidance and consideration of internal capacity constraints, especially in smaller country offices. While largely achieved, some areas lacked coherence and clarity. Though considerable effort went into the plan's development, implementation takes time and advance planning. Therefore, the evaluation recommends UNFPA to operationalize acceleration by clarifying and strengthening linkages between concepts and programming approaches well before the next Strategic Plan's launch. Fourth, a clearer approach to acceleration in the next Strategic Plan and the Country Programs is needed to enhance coherence across UNFPA initiatives, align modes of engagement, and guide human resources priorities at the country level. While all strategic shifts are relevant, some, like normative work and ICBD financing, require new or improved strategies and capacity building due to their shifts in emphasis and direction. Therefore, the evaluation recommends strengthening capacities to support acceleration, especially in normative work, funding to finance, knowledge management, and strategic communication. Lastly, UNFPA has improved its humanitarian response capacity, but needs clearer guidance and strategic integration to implement resilience, humanitarian, development, and peace efforts within resource constraints. UNFPA also needs to review its skill set to ensure a capacity for both normative and advocacy work and humanitarian crisis response. Therefore, the evaluation recommends better integration of humanitarian, development and peace-responsive interventions, considering UNFPA's diverse and evolving operating context. Mr. President, distinguished delegates, I trust this evaluation evidence and insights will guide in adjusting the current Strategic Plan and developing the new one, accelerating the achievements towards the 3 transformative results. This concludes my presentation, Mr. President. I thank the Executive Board for its support and welcome any questions. Thank you very much.
